blocks.text: The chapter begins by rejecting the idea that God has cast off Israel. Paul identifies himself as an Israelite and uses Elijah’s story of a preserved remnant to frame the present situation: grace, not works, explains the remnant. He then insists that Israel’s stumbling is not a final fall, relating gentile inclusion to Israel’s future fullness. The later reference to a partial hardening should therefore not be read as a permanent racial curse or as a basis for gentile arrogance.

The olive-tree image addresses gentile readers directly. Wild branches are grafted among the natural branches and share the root’s nourishment; they do not support the root or gain ownership over it. The warning against boasting is reinforced by the possibility that natural branches may be grafted in again. Thus the metaphor does not portray Jews as permanently discarded or gentile Christians as their ethnic replacement.

“All Israel will be saved” in verse 26 has major disputed questions about both its referent and timing. Proposed readings include corporate Israel in a future turn, a remnant across time, or another understanding of the whole. The chapter itself places this difficult statement beside its anti-boasting warning and its declaration that Israel remains beloved because of the ancestors and that God’s gifts and calling are irrevocable.

The chapter’s movement from partial hardening to mercy calls for humility rather than certainty about controlling God’s judgment. Its language of “enemies” in relation to the gospel is immediately set alongside beloved status, irrevocable calling, and mercy toward both Jews and gentiles. These tensions neither erase disagreement nor license collective hatred, contempt, forced conversion, or claims of permanent Jewish abandonment.

Questions about Romans’ textual transmission require careful judgment. An automated validation result, retrieval score, confessional popularity, or manuscript count does not itself constitute human approval. P46 is an early and extensive witness to Paul’s letters, but it is not the original manuscript; its readings must be compared with other Greek and versional witnesses.
